title=One-word and two-word comparisons
body=красне́е — redder. бо́лее до́брый — kinder. The first is a short comparative with an ending expressing a higher degree of redness; this short form does not change for gender, number or case. The second combines a word meaning more with the ordinary long adjective meaning kind. In this two-word construction the adjective still changes for agreement. Not every adjective has a one-word comparative, and these examples do not give a complete formation rule for unfamiliar adjectives.

title=Comparative versus superlative
body=наибо́льший — the biggest. This retained superlative identifies the greatest size in the relevant group, rather than just a greater degree. Contrast the source labels бо́лее — more, ме́нее — less, and наиме́нее — least. More and less express comparison; least identifies the lowest degree. For наибо́льший select the biggest, not more or less. For бо́лее до́брый select kinder, not least or bigger. These choices recognize existing forms; they do not assess independently forming new comparisons or a complete comparison sentence.

kind=TEACH
title=Questions selecting an apple or a book
body=Которое яблоко моё? — Which apple is mine? Которую книгу вы хотите? — Which book do you want? These are direct questions asking which member is selected, not relative clauses modifying an earlier noun. In the apple question the selecting form agrees with a neuter singular subject in the nominative. In the book question it agrees with a feminine singular direct object in the accusative. Match the whole question: ownership of an apple differs from wanting a book.

kind=TEACH
title=A relative clause adds information about a noun
body=Человек, который изменил мир — The man who changed the world. The clause following the comma describes the preceding person; it does not ask which person. The relative form takes masculine singular agreement from that noun, and nominative case because it is the subject of changed inside its own clause. For a relative form, gender and number come from the noun it describes; case comes from the role inside the relative clause, not automatically from the preceding noun.

kind=TEACH
title=With whom: a preposition inside the relative clause
body=Же́нщина, с кото́рой я дружу́ — The woman (who) I'm friends with. The relative clause describes the woman. Its relative form has feminine singular agreement and instrumental case after the preposition meaning with. Russian keeps this preposition before the relative form, while the retained English rendering places with at the end. Compare the woman described by friendship with the man described by changing the world and the two direct questions. Recognizing these meanings does not demonstrate independently choosing a relative case or producing a new clause.

бо́льший — bigger. лу́чший — better. These retained forms concern degree of a quality, rather than naming an unrelated object. The first compares size. The second is the source gloss used by the existing choice; it can mean best in context, so better here is not a universal translation. These full adjective forms can change for gender, number and case; they are not the same construction as an unchanging short comparative. Qualified review of the contextual gloss remains pending.

красне́е — redder. бо́лее до́брый — kinder. The first is a short comparative with an ending expressing a higher degree of redness; this short form does not change for gender, number or case. The second combines a word meaning more with the ordinary long adjective meaning kind. In this two-word construction the adjective still changes for agreement. Not every adjective has a one-word comparative, and these examples do not give a complete formation rule for unfamiliar adjectives.

наибо́льший — the biggest. This retained superlative identifies the greatest size in the relevant group, rather than just a greater degree. Contrast the source labels бо́лее — more, ме́нее — less, and наиме́нее — least. More and less express comparison; least identifies the lowest degree. For наибо́льший select the biggest, not more or less. For бо́лее до́брый select kinder, not least or bigger. These choices recognize existing forms; they do not assess independently forming new comparisons or a complete comparison sentence.

Которое яблоко моё? — Which apple is mine? Которую книгу вы хотите? — Which book do you want? These are direct questions asking which member is selected, not relative clauses modifying an earlier noun. In the apple question the selecting form agrees with a neuter singular subject in the nominative. In the book question it agrees with a feminine singular direct object in the accusative. Match the whole question: ownership of an apple differs from wanting a book.

Человек, который изменил мир — The man who changed the world. The clause following the comma describes the preceding person; it does not ask which person. The relative form takes masculine singular agreement from that noun, and nominative case because it is the subject of changed inside its own clause. For a relative form, gender and number come from the noun it describes; case comes from the role inside the relative clause, not automatically from the preceding noun.

Же́нщина, с кото́рой я дружу́ — The woman (who) I'm friends with. The relative clause describes the woman. Its relative form has feminine singular agreement and instrumental case after the preposition meaning with. Russian keeps this preposition before the relative form, while the retained English rendering places with at the end. Compare the woman described by friendship with the man described by changing the world and the two direct questions. Recognizing these meanings does not demonstrate independently choosing a relative case or producing a new clause.

originalSourceText=forms are usual only for qualitative adjectives and adverbs. Comparative and superlative synthetic forms are not part of the [[Linguistic paradigm|paradigm]] of original adjective but are different lexical items, since not all qualitative adjectives have them. A few adjectives have irregular forms that are declined as usual adjectives: большо́й 'big' – бо́льший 'bigger', хоро́ший 'good' – лу́чший 'better'. Most synthetically-derived comparative forms are derived by adding the suffix -е́е or -е́й to the adjective stem: кра́сный 'red' – красне́е 'redder'; these forms are difficult to distinguish from adverbs, whose comparative forms often coincide with those of their adjectival counterparts.<ref name=Belo /> Superlative synthetic forms are derived by adding the suffix -е́йш- or -а́йш- and additionally sometimes the prefix наи-, or using a special comparative form with the prefix наи-: до́брый 'kind' – добре́йший 'the kindest', большо́й 'big' – наибо́льший 'the biggest'.

An alternative is to add an adverb to the positive form of the adjective. The adverbs used for this are бо́лее 'more' / ме́нее 'less' and са́мый 'most' / наибо́лее 'most' / наиме́нее 'least': for example, до́брый 'kind' – бо́лее до́брый 'kinder' – са́мый до́брый 'the kindest'. This way is rarely used if special comparative forms exist.

originalSourceText=forms are usual only for qualitative adjectives and adverbs. Comparative and superlative synthetic forms are not part of the [[Linguistic paradigm|paradigm]] of original adjective but are different lexical items, since not all qualitative adjectives have them. A few adjectives have irregular forms that are declined as usual adjectives: большо́й 'big' – бо́льший 'bigger', хоро́ший 'good' – лу́чший 'better'. Most synthetically-derived comparative forms are derived by adding the suffix -е́е or -е́й to the adjective stem: кра́сный 'red' – красне́е 'redder'; these forms are difficult to distinguish from adverbs, whose comparative forms often coincide with those of their adjectival counterparts.<ref name=Belo /> Superlative synthetic forms are derived by adding the suffix -е́йш- or -а́йш- and additionally sometimes the prefix наи-, or using a special comparative form with the prefix наи-: до́брый 'kind' – добре́йший 'the kindest', большо́й 'big' – наибо́льший 'the biggest'.

An alternative is to add an adverb to the positive form of the adjective. The adverbs used for this are бо́лее 'more' / ме́нее 'less' and са́мый 'most' / наибо́лее 'most' / наиме́нее 'least': for example, до́брый 'kind' – бо́лее до́брый 'kinder' – са́мый до́брый 'the kindest'. This way is rarely used if special comparative forms exist.

originalSourceText=forms are usual only for qualitative adjectives and adverbs. Comparative and superlative synthetic forms are not part of the [[Linguistic paradigm|paradigm]] of original adjective but are different lexical items, since not all qualitative adjectives have them. A few adjectives have irregular forms that are declined as usual adjectives: большо́й 'big' – бо́льший 'bigger', хоро́ший 'good' – лу́чший 'better'. Most synthetically-derived comparative forms are derived by adding the suffix -е́е or -е́й to the adjective stem: кра́сный 'red' – красне́е 'redder'; these forms are difficult to distinguish from adverbs, whose comparative forms often coincide with those of their adjectival counterparts.<ref name=Belo /> Superlative synthetic forms are derived by adding the suffix -е́йш- or -а́йш- and additionally sometimes the prefix наи-, or using a special comparative form with the prefix наи-: до́брый 'kind' – добре́йший 'the kindest', большо́й 'big' – наибо́льший 'the biggest'.

An alternative is to add an adverb to the positive form of the adjective. The adverbs used for this are бо́лее 'more' / ме́нее 'less' and са́мый 'most' / наибо́лее 'most' / наиме́нее 'least': for example, до́брый 'kind' – бо́лее до́брый 'kinder' – са́мый до́брый 'the kindest'. This way is rarely used if special comparative forms exist.

originalSourceText=forms are usual only for qualitative adjectives and adverbs. Comparative and superlative synthetic forms are not part of the [[Linguistic paradigm|paradigm]] of original adjective but are different lexical items, since not all qualitative adjectives have them. A few adjectives have irregular forms that are declined as usual adjectives: большо́й 'big' – бо́льший 'bigger', хоро́ший 'good' – лу́чший 'better'. Most synthetically-derived comparative forms are derived by adding the suffix -е́е or -е́й to the adjective stem: кра́сный 'red' – красне́е 'redder'; these forms are difficult to distinguish from adverbs, whose comparative forms often coincide with those of their adjectival counterparts.<ref name=Belo /> Superlative synthetic forms are derived by adding the suffix -е́йш- or -а́йш- and additionally sometimes the prefix наи-, or using a special comparative form with the prefix наи-: до́брый 'kind' – добре́йший 'the kindest', большо́й 'big' – наибо́льший 'the biggest'.

An alternative is to add an adverb to the positive form of the adjective. The adverbs used for this are бо́лее 'more' / ме́нее 'less' and са́мый 'most' / наибо́лее 'most' / наиме́нее 'least': for example, до́брый 'kind' – бо́лее до́брый 'kinder' – са́мый до́брый 'the kindest'. This way is rarely used if special comparative forms exist.

originalSourceText=forms are usual only for qualitative adjectives and adverbs. Comparative and superlative synthetic forms are not part of the [[Linguistic paradigm|paradigm]] of original adjective but are different lexical items, since not all qualitative adjectives have them. A few adjectives have irregular forms that are declined as usual adjectives: большо́й 'big' – бо́льший 'bigger', хоро́ший 'good' – лу́чший 'better'. Most synthetically-derived comparative forms are derived by adding the suffix -е́е or -е́й to the adjective stem: кра́сный 'red' – красне́е 'redder'; these forms are difficult to distinguish from adverbs, whose comparative forms often coincide with those of their adjectival counterparts.<ref name=Belo /> Superlative synthetic forms are derived by adding the suffix -е́йш- or -а́йш- and additionally sometimes the prefix наи-, or using a special comparative form with the prefix наи-: до́брый 'kind' – добре́йший 'the kindest', большо́й 'big' – наибо́льший 'the biggest'.

An alternative is to add an adverb to the positive form of the adjective. The adverbs used for this are бо́лее 'more' / ме́нее 'less' and са́мый 'most' / наибо́лее 'most' / наиме́нее 'least': for example, до́брый 'kind' – бо́лее до́брый 'kinder' – са́мый до́брый 'the kindest'. This way is rarely used if special comparative forms exist.
